title: Plagiarism
must: Presenting another person's work, words, ideas, images or code as your own without acknowledging the source; academic dishonesty, can also break copyright.

title: Source, citation and academic integrity
must: A source is any work information is taken from; a citation says who created it, when and where to find it; academic integrity = own work, every source acknowledged, task rules followed.

title: Forms of plagiarism
must: At least three: copy-paste, patchwriting / mosaic, paraphrasing without citing, self-plagiarism, buying / ghost-writing, collusion, AI-generated text presented as own, code copying.

title: Why it is a problem and consequences
must: Dishonest, unfair, no learning; consequences at school (zero, redo), in exams (disqualification), at university (fail, expulsion), at work (reputation, legal action).

title: Why people plagiarise
must: Lack of time / planning, not knowing how to cite or paraphrase, thinking Internet content is free, pressure for marks.

title: Anti-plagiarism resource
must: A program / service that compares a document with a large database (web, books, journals, submitted work) and produces a similarity report.

title: How a document is checked
must: Text split into fragments / fingerprints (hashes), compared with the databases, matches highlighted and linked to sources; code checkers compare structure, not just text.

title: Examples of resources
must: At least two named checkers (e.g. Turnitin, Antiplagiat, Unicheck, Plagiarism Checker, MOSS) and free online checker vs institutional service.

title: Similarity score
must: Percentage of text matching the databases; originality = 100 % − similarity; it measures matching text, not plagiarism.

title: Limitations of checkers
must: Cannot detect sources not in the database, fooled by heavy paraphrasing / synonym tools / translation, cannot decide whether a match is cited, allowed or understood.

title: Reading a similarity report
must: Parts: overall score, highlighted matches, list of sources with percentages; judge each match — properly quoted and cited, common phrase / bibliography, or plagiarism.

title: Interpreting the score
must: High score can be fine (quotes, bibliography, technical terms), low score can still hide plagiarism; exclude quotes / bibliography; the teacher decides.

title: Checking your own work
must: Steps before submitting: run a checker, look at each match, add quotation marks / citations or paraphrase, check again.

title: Checking without a dedicated service
must: Search a sentence in quotation marks, reverse image search, code-similarity tool.
